title: Dhruva's handful of husks
hookLine: Dhruva does tapas for a throne higher than anyone's, then finds his wish was husks
carry: santosha: nothing is higher than enough
tomorrow: The serpent who holds the world

cards: A little boy, Dhruva, five years old, tries to climb onto his father's lap. His half-brother is already sitting there. His stepmother pulls him away: you weren't born from me, she says, so you don't belong there.
If you want that seat, pray to God to be born as my son. Dhruva runs crying to his mother. She doesn't argue.
She tells him only the Lord can take away a pain like this. So the boy walks into the forest, alone, to ask God for a throne higher than anyone's.

teach.h: A MANTRA, AND MONTHS IN THE FOREST.
teach.b: In the Bhagavata Purana, the sage Narada meets him on the road and gives him a mantra: om namo bhagavate vasudevaya. Dhruva repeats it for months, living on fruit, then leaves, then water, then air.
And Vishnu appears. The boy gets what he came for: a kingdom, and a place in the sky that never moves, the pole star. But the Bhagavata says something surprising.
Dhruva wasn't happy with his own wish.
He felt like someone who had pleased an emperor and asked him for a handful of husks. Many teachers read it this way: he'd met the Lord, and he'd asked for a chair. That's sutra 2.42 in a story.
From contentment, santosha, comes unsurpassed happiness: anuttama, nothing higher, nothing above it.

The classical commentary quotes an old verse: whatever pleasure desire brings in this world, and whatever great pleasure there is in heaven, together they aren't worth a sixteenth of the happiness that comes when craving ends.
And contentment here isn't settling. The commentary calls it not wanting more than what's at hand. The wanting that began on his father's lap was the wound, not the missing chair.
Around this line, Patanjali gives the other observances' fruits: from study, meeting your chosen deity; from surrender to Ishvara, samadhi. Many Hindus still call the pole star Dhruva.
Point to it tonight, and you're pointing at a boy who found something with nothing above it.

how: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often single out santosha as a daily practice of accepting what is at hand; Dhruva's story is a favorite with Hindu children, many Hindus call the pole star Dhruva, and some link contentment to offering food to God before eating and receiving it back as prasad.

o: a reward for strict discipline, given by the gods
unsurpassed: a happiness with nothing above it
a happiness that comes only after death, in heaven

games.q: each observance and its fruit — tap the pairs.

s: contentment here means settling for less
the commentary means not wanting more than what's at hand. it isn't settling; the craving for more is what goes.
after meeting Vishnu, Dhruva was thrilled with what he'd asked for
the Bhagavata says he felt like someone who pleased an emperor and asked for a handful of husks.
the commentary says desire's pleasures aren't worth a sixteenth of craving's end
an old verse quoted on 2.42 says even heaven's pleasures don't come close.

games.q: your best friend gets the big gift you wanted, and you feel like Dhruva watching his half-brother on the lap. where does 2.42 put the happiness with nothing above it?
o: in getting a bigger gift next time.
at the end of wanting more than what's at hand.
games.why: 2.42 gives unsurpassed happiness to contentment, and the commentary puts it at the end of craving, beyond even heaven's pleasures. Dhruva saw it the moment he met the Lord, and his wish looked like husks.

practice: Notice one thing that's already here and already enough: the breath arriving without being asked, the chair holding you up, a little warmth in your hands.

When the mind starts listing what's missing, notice the list and come back to what's enough. If you pray, you can repeat a name of God slowly, as Dhruva did. You don't have to feel blissful; just let enough be enough.

wordCard.voice: Anuttama, unsurpassed, nothing higher. Sutra 2.42: from contentment, santosha, a happiness with nothing above it.

orig.note: Sanskrit santoṣa: contentment, satisfaction; the second niyama, whose fruit in 2.42 is unsurpassed happiness.

carryVoice: Your line: santosha, nothing is higher than enough. Dhruva met the Lord and saw his wish was a handful of husks. That's day four sixty-one.
